blocks.content: Every join covered so far combined two genuinely different tables, customers and orders. A self join takes a different approach entirely, joining a single table with itself, treating it as two separate copies within the same query.

This topic covers why a self join needs two aliases for the same table, a worked example using an employees table with a manager_id column, finding peer rows that genuinely share a value, and a common mistake that silently loses the top of a hierarchy.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784364194927-405890769.png
blocks.alt: A self join combines a table with itself, rather than combining two genuinely different tables

blocks.content: 1. What a Self Join Actually Is
blocks.text: 1. What a Self Join Actually Is

blocks.content: A self join is genuinely just a regular join where both sides happen to be the same table. This comes up whenever a table stores a reference to another row in that same table, like an employees table where each row has a manager_id pointing at another employee row.
Without a self join, answering who manages whom would require a separate lookup table. With one, the hierarchy already living inside a single table can be queried directly.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784364196854-729986438.png
blocks.alt: A self join pairs each employee row with the row their manager_id genuinely points to, all within one table

blocks.content: 2. Why Self Join Needs Two Aliases
blocks.text: 2. Why Self Join Needs Two Aliases

blocks.content: Since both sides of a self join come from the exact same table, the database genuinely cannot tell them apart without two separate aliases. One alias represents the employee side of the relationship, the other represents the manager side.
These aliases are not optional labeling, they are the only way to reference employee columns and manager columns separately when both sets of columns technically come from the same underlying table.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784364198577-55201271.png
blocks.alt: The same employees table is aliased twice, once as the employee side and once as the manager side

blocks.content: {"headers":["Alias","Represents"],"rows":[["e","The employee row being described"],["m","The manager row that e.manager_id genuinely points to"]]}
3. A Worked Example

Suppose the employees table has an id column and a manager_id column, where manager_id stores the id of that employee genuine manager, another row in the same table. Pairing each employee with their manager name needs a self join.
This query genuinely reads as joining the employee side, aliased e, against the manager side, aliased m, matching each employee row to the specific row representing their manager.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784364200175-795364558.png
blocks.alt: A worked example: self joining employees against itself pairs each employee with their own manager name

blocks.content: 4. A Genuine Gotcha With the Top of a Hierarchy
blocks.text: 4. A Genuine Gotcha With the Top of a Hierarchy

blocks.content: An inner join self join silently excludes the employee at the very top of the hierarchy, since that row genuinely has no manager_id at all. Switching to a left join keeps that top level employee, showing a NULL manager name instead of dropping the row.
This is exactly the same left join behavior covered earlier, just applied to a self join instead of two genuinely different tables.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784364201725-171104781.png
blocks.alt: An inner join self join excludes the top of the hierarchy entirely; a left join keeps that row with a NULL manager

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Whether to use inner join or left join for a self join depends entirely on whether the row with no genuine self reference, the top manager here, should still appear in the result.
5. Finding Peer Rows That Share a Value
blocks.text: 5. Finding Peer Rows That Share a Value

blocks.content: A self join is also genuinely useful for finding pairs of rows within the same table that share a value, like employees who report to the same manager, without pairing an employee with themselves or producing the same pair twice in reverse order.

SELECT e1.name, e2.name
FROM employees e1
JOIN employees e2 ON e1.manager_id=e2.manager_id
AND e1.id<e2.id;
blocks.code:
SELECT e1.name, e2.name
FROM employees e1
JOIN employees e2 ON e1.manager_id=e2.manager_id
AND e1.id<e2.id;

codes.sql:
SELECT e1.name, e2.name
FROM employees e1
JOIN employees e2 ON e1.manager_id=e2.manager_id
AND e1.id<e2.id;

blocks.content: The e1.id less than e2.id condition genuinely does two things at once, it prevents an employee from being paired with themselves, and it prevents the same pair from appearing twice with the two names simply reversed.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784364203281-616224228.png
blocks.alt: A self join with an id comparison finds peer employees sharing the same manager, without self pairs or reversed duplicates

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: Dropping the id comparison from a peer finding self join genuinely produces every employee paired with themselves, plus every real pair listed twice in both directions.
6. Genuinely Common Mistakes

A few real patterns undermine self join usage. Forgetting to alias the table twice, which the database rejects outright since it cannot tell which copy a column reference belongs to. Using inner join for a hierarchy query and silently losing the top level row.
And omitting the id comparison when finding peer rows, which produces self pairs and duplicate reversed pairs that a genuine peer comparison should never include.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784364204844-333099233.png
blocks.alt: Common mistakes: forgetting to alias twice, losing the top of the hierarchy, and missing the id comparison for peer rows
